articles.title: China's big political meeting could see Xi 'tighten discipline' in party
articles.summary: The highly secretive four-day Plenum starts Monday in Beijing.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Plenums are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year By Stephen McDonell 
China correspondent 
- Published 26 October 2026 
A major political gathering is under way in the Chinese capital, with a closed-door meeting of senior figures that could shape the look of the ruling Communist Party in the years to come. 
The Fifth Plenum brings together around 300 members of the Central Committee and state media said it would pave the way for a "tightening of discipline" within the Party's ranks. 
The four-day session that started on Monday will give Xi Jinping an opportunity to further consolidate his grip on power following recent purges. 
The normally annual plenums are highly secretive, but a summary of decisions and a more detailed document will be made public after. 
What is a plenum? 
They are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year. 
There are usually seven plenums during each five-year Central Committee term and they are watched from afar because they are meant to signal the leadership's priorities. 
The timing for this year's gathering is important because it is a year away from the next Party Congress, where a new set of priorities is set up and a new central committee appointed. 
Officially, the Central Committee selects the Party's top leadership but the real processes leading to the selection are kept secret within the Party elite. 
The next Party Congress will almost certainly reappoint Xi as the country's leader, following the abolition of term limits. 
What is on the agenda this year? 
Past plenum sessions have been used to declare Xi as "the core" of the Party, abolish term limits which cleared the way for him to remain in power indefinitely, and elevate his personal philosophy – branded as "Xi Jinping Thought" – to the same level as Chairman Mao. 
This year's plenum is an opportunity for Xi to dictate strategy in the run up to the Congress, ensuring that views are aligned and delegates loyal. 
Even the location of the meeting, which will wrap up on Thursday, has not been announced. Past plenums have been held inside Beijing's Jingxi Hotel. 
According to a readout from the powerful 21-member Politburo this September, the plenum will adopt a decision on "several major issues persistently advancing the comprehensive strict governance of the Party", which is being read as a way to further ensure obedience and effectiveness from distant party officials. 
This means it would also be a time of nervousness for delegates as they look around the room with its "empty chairs" following the scale of recent purges within the Party. 
Allegations of corruption, even "moral corruption", have seen large swathes of senior figures culled. 
"Moral corruption" has been seen by experts as a way of cracking down on perceived disloyalty to Xi because overall disloyalty to the Party can be interpreted as a breach of "morality". 
The Asia Society Policy Institute has estimated that of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022 only two have not been taken down. 
The all-powerful seven-man Central Military Commission, which runs the armed forces in China, has also been whittled down to only two people, Xi Jinping and one other general. 
This plenum is an opportunity for him to appoint new officers to this body.

articles.title: Hundreds of flights cancelled as Typhoon Champi shuts Taiwan
articles.summary: One person has died after being swept away by waves in Taiwan's Liuqiu island, authorities say.
articles.full_text:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, 
Taiwan is bracing for Champi's worst effects on Saturday By Koh Ewe 
- Published 23 October 2026 
Hundreds of flights in the East Asia region were cancelled on Friday as powerful Typhoon Champi roared close to Taiwan's north-east coast. 
Schools and offices in Taiwan were shut as Champi neared the island. While it is uncertain if it will make landfall, the storm was forecast to bring 90cm (35in) of rain and strong winds to the north-east until Saturday. 
One person died after being swept away by waves, authorities said. The storm also injured 171 people and forced 1,000 others to evacuate. 
Champi is the latest in a string of intense typhoons as a Super El Niño heats up the Pacific Ocean and fuels storms. At its peak earlier this week, it was the planet's strongest storm of the year so far. 
On Friday afternoon, Champi was packing wind gusts of 191km/h (119mph) . 
After passing Taiwan's north-eastern tip and the Okinawa islands in southern Japan, Champi is expected to hover over the waters off China's eastern coast, before curving farther to the north-east to Japan's main island. 
Weather agencies in Taiwan, Hong Kong and Japan forecast that the eye of the storm is expected to pass without making landfall in Taiwan. 
However, a forecaster in Taiwan's Central Weather Administration told Reuters that they could not rule this out completely - especially if the storm "stalls, loops or wobbles from side to side" as it approaches. 
Rainfall is expected to peak on Saturday morning and continue to batter Taiwan until Saturday evening, the Central Weather Administration said. 
Taiwanese authorities have urged people to stay away from coasts and mountains. 
Work and classes were suspended in nearly all of Taiwan's 22 counties and cities on Friday - what's colloquially known as a "typhoon holiday" - as Champi approached the island. 
Taiwan's $5tn (£3.7tn) stock exchange was also closed on Friday because of the severe weather. 
Only Kinmen county, an archipelago located to the west of Taiwan's main island, continued work and classes as usual. 
In Japan, power cuts were reported in nearly 8,400 households in the southern Okinawa prefecture, according to the local power company. 
More than 160 flights have been cancelled across four Japanese airlines. 
Champi has also stirred up heavy rains and winds in Batanes, a Philippine island chain below southern Taiwan. 
Photos posted on the local government's Facebook page showed waves crashing into seaside villages and roads closed to traffic. There were no immediate reports of casualties. 
Typhoon Champi became the strongest storm of the year earlier this week, when it attained a maximum sustained wind speed of 185mph (298km/h) as it moved over the Philippine Sea - the equivalent of a Category 5 hurricane. 
While initially categorised as a "super typhoon", Champi weakened on Wednesday as it continued barrelling through the sea. 
This is shaping up to be one of the most active typhoon seasons the region has seen in years. Champi is Japan's 30th typhoon of the year - making this the first time since 2013 that the country has seen so many storms. 
The recent frequency of storms is due to an unusually strong El Niño - a naturally occurring phenomenon that hits the Pacific Ocean every few years and can trigger extreme weather events, from droughts to typhoons.

articles.title: Powerful earthquake hits Tibet killing 16 people, reports say
articles.summary: The quake hit a mountainous, sparsely-populated area in what China calls the Tibet Autonomous Region.
articles.full_text:
By Laura Bicker ,  China correspondent,   and   Harry Sekulich 
- Published 23 October 2026 
A magnitude 7.0 earthquake has hit a mountainous region in Tibet, killing at least 16 people and injuring dozens, according to Chinese state media. 
The centre of the quake hit Baqên County in the Nagqu region on Thursday night, Xinhua reported, citing the local emergency management bureau. 
The county - located in what China calls the Tibet Autonomous Region after annexing it in the 1950s - is 400km (250 miles) north-east of the region's capital, Lhasa. 
Authorities have declared the incident an emergency and deployed rescue teams to the affected area, where 65 others have been injured, including 11 people with severe injuries. 
The electricity supply has been cut off and 339 homes have collapsed in the affected region, though by Friday morning there were reports of power restored in some areas. 
Local media said more than 12,400 people had been relocated following the earthquake. 
Rockfall has forced roads in the region to close, making it more difficult for crews to reach impacted high-altitude areas. 
The US Geological Survey (USGS) has recorded seven tremors close to the epicentre, all of which are located in the mountainous region. The largest tremor was recorded at 5.2 magnitude at a depth of 10km. 
Shallow earthquakes and tremors closer to the Earth's surface are more damaging than deep quakes. 
Figure caption, 
Rescuers search through rubble after Tibet earthquake 
Several survivors of the earthquake have told local media about their harrowing escape. 
Nagqu resident Yixi Cuomu told Tibet Daily that she was asleep in her bed when her house started shaking violently. Realising it was an earthquake, she headed outside barefoot, her "legs trembling uncontrollably" as she descended the staircase in her home. 
Another eyewitness said the shaking was so violent "that in that moment I felt as if several hundred yaks were running past us". 
Residents chose to spend the night outdoors in subzero temperatures, seeking shelter in tents or their cars, as they feared aftershocks could trap them in their homes, according to the news outlet. 
Chinese state media reported on Friday morning that more than 400 aftershocks had been registered since the quake occurred. 
China's Premier Li Qiang has called for "urgent efforts" to organise rescue operations and medical treatment for the injured, and relocate and resettle affected residents appropriately, according to state media. 
Li noted that the earthquake-hit area is at a high altitude, around 4,800m (15,750ft), and prone to aftershocks. 
The Ministry of Emergency Management has dispatched a working group to the affected area to guide rescue and disaster relief operations. 
Separately, the Chinese government announced it was allocating 50 million yuan (£5.6m; $7.5m) for disaster relief efforts in Tibet. 
Image source, CCTV via Reuters Image caption, 
Firefighters are seen helping residents injured by the quake in Baqên, Tibet 
Videos on social media of the moment the quake struck show villagers running into the streets as buildings shake violently in the dark. These have not been independently verified. 
The region is prone to devastating seismic activity. 
In 2023, a 6.2 magnitude quake killed more than 120 people in the nearby mountainous Gansu province of China. 
Tibet and Nepal were also recently devastated by massive floods and landslides less than two months ago, unleashed by a glacier collapse, which killed at least 1,400 people. Hundreds of others are still reported missing. 
Despite the region presenting some of the most challenging rescue conditions, rescue teams on the Tibetan plateau are highly experienced and have shown an ability to mobilise quickly. 
In January 2025, military personnel, firefighters, police and specialist rescue teams were in the area within hours after a powerful eartquake struck the Shigatse region of Tibet. 
The Chinese military also have drones to help survey the area. 
Tibet, which has long demanded greater autonomy, is one of the most tightly controlled regions in China. 
With foreign media restricted from the region and information heavily censored by authorities, Chinese state media is the main source for updates and details when such disasters happen.

articles.title: Britain's posh schools are heading to India for students and profits
articles.summary: Half a dozen elite British schools are chasing growth in India amid a boom in its  wealthy population.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Harrow School, Bengaluru Image caption, 
At Harrow's Bengaluru campus, students wear the traditional Harrow hats and uniforms By Nikhil Inamdar Mumbai 
- Published 24 October 2026 
On the outskirts of Chandigarh city in India's north-western Punjab state, a 473-year-old legacy British public school opened its first all-girls international campus earlier this year. 
In contrast to the prominent Gothic-style central building on the school grounds in Bedfordshire, England, the Indian premises are more modern, with purpose-built academic blocks. But a conspicuous red-brick clock tower bears the imprint of the school's British heritage. 
The Bedford School, Mohali, is the newest in at least half a dozen British public schools (elite, fee-paying private schools with a long history), including three of the country's oldest, that have set up shop across the length and breadth of India. Their expansion comes amid tighter market conditions in China and the introduction of VAT on private school fees in Britain from 1 January 2025. 
Since 2023, Bengaluru - India's Silicon Valley and a hub of software and start-up companies - has been home to the prestigious Harrow School, alma mater of India's first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru. Queen Elizabeth's School launched in Gurugram near the capital Delhi this August. Shrewsbury School has a campus in Bhopal in central India, while Wellington College has chosen to set up base in Pune, a western city that calls itself the "Oxford of the East" for its well-regarded universities and colleges. 
Millfield and a few others are reportedly on their way with satellite campuses in the coming years. 
For decades, India has been home to well-established local boarding schools modelled on the colonial British public-school system, serving elite, aristocratic families. But this market has rapidly expanded with newly wealthy Indian families increasingly aspiring to give their children more global exposure. 
"Our international curriculum is quite a driver for many of them," Caroline Pascoe, head of school at Harrow in Bengaluru, told the BBC. 
Harrow and Bedford are among the few schools in India that follow an all-through Cambridge curriculum - a global education framework recognised at 10,000 schools worldwide - from primary through to A-levels. 
Image source, Bedford School, Mohali Image caption, 
Bedford School is the latest in at least half a dozen British public schools that have entered India 
Harsimran Singh Kocchar, whose own extended family runs a chain of schools across India, says he decided to send his five-year old daughter Parineet to Bedford Mohali because of the "holistic focus of the school on character development, confidence and not merely academics". 
He said he was also drawn to the fact the school did not have a "VIP culture" unlike many Indian equivalents. 
"All kids are treated the same. Children of ministers and bureaucrats don't get greater privileges," said Singh. 
Beyond the growing ranks of well-heeled local families, non-resident Indians who have either returned home after long stints abroad, or those still in the UK or Middle East wanting their children to connect to their roots, are also a significant market for these schools, says Pascoe. 
Sixty per cent of Harrow's staff in Bengaluru are international and, like the others, it has imported its unique traditions to its Bengaluru campus: teachers are called Beaks, and students wear the traditional Harrow hats and uniform and take part in The Long Ducker - a cross-country race that happens across its schools globally. There is also a house system - a hallmark of traditional British education. 
These quintessentially parochial quirks are blended with local customs such as singing the Indian national anthem every morning or celebrating Ganesh Chaturthi, a major Hindu festival. 
Image source, Harrow School, Bengaluru Image caption, 
Schools such as Harrow in Bengaluru promote extracurricular activities like music and drama 
While India's growing economic credentials and burgeoning population of newly minted millionaires are a natural tailwind for expansion, this growth is partly being driven by a slowdown in China. 
Much of the expansion of British public schools abroad in the past decade was driven by China and Hong Kong - half of the 151 satellite campuses operated by 50 UK schools are situated in these countries. 
But that growth has slowed following changes in regulation, and "increased scrutiny, and even resistance, from national governments", according to a 2025 study by the UK-based Private Education Policy Forum ( PEPF , external ) think tank. 
A new 2024 Chinese law that required schools to integrate patriotic education into all subjects further challenged expansion and even led to planned campuses being cancelled, prompting these schools to consider other locations like India and Vietnam, according to PEPF. 
Moreover, in the 2024 Autumn Budget, Britain introduced a 20% VAT on private school fees. Naomi Atkins, founding principal at Bedford School Mohali, says this has forced many private schools to look overseas. 
"They are in a desperate situation. Even those that hadn't previously looked for international expansion are now suddenly active in India," she told the BBC. 
Image source, Harrow School, Bengaluru Image caption, 
Well-heeled local families and non-resident Indians are a major target market for British schools in India 
But India has not been an easy market, she admits. 
Most of these schools are set up in partnership with local investors or operators. 
While in the past schools in other countries might have been able to do deals at 10% of revenue - the fee that they would charge the local partner-investor - margins in India may have shrunk to as low as 1% in some cases, says Atikins. 
There has also been some over-estimation of the size of the market, she says. 
Even though India has nearly 250 million children enrolled in schools, English education is deeply entrenched in the country and competition from local players is much more intense compared with other non-English speaking countries like China, Korea or Vietnam. 
India's per capita income is also far lower and the high price-points of the British schools - which can charge up to £15,000 or more for full boarding - can limit growth. 
"I've worked in Indonesia, Malaysia and China but Indians are much more price-sensitive - they like a bargain," says Atkins. 
That is why Bedford Mohali has set its fees at roughly half those charged by other British schools. 
Between 2011-12 and 2022-23, the satellite campuses of British schools generated £152.4m in profit, according to PEPF, and this profit has grown substantially over the years. 
But in India, it appears growth is likely to be slow and steady rather than explosive. 
The country's old colonial roots and new money afford the legacy institutions a significant business opportunity, but it is unlikely to be big enough to offset the loss of the Chinese market, at least immediately.

articles.title: Lula wins fourth term in dramatic Brazil election comeback
articles.summary: The left-wing incumbent president had lost the first round to right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro.
articles.full_text:
Figure caption, 
By Ione Wells ,  Reporting from Brasília   and   Hafsa Khalil 
- Published 26 October 2026 
Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a fourth term in office in a dramatic comeback over his right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro. 
Left-wing leader Lula took 51.79% of votes, becoming the first president since Brazil's return to civilian rule in 1985 to be elected after losing the first round of voting. 
Lula told jubilant crowds his victory was a "loss for negativity, lies", adding "long live democracy". 
Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, has so far refused to recognise the result and called for it to be annulled. World leaders have congratulated Lula on his re-election. 
Bolsonaro's rejection comes as no surprise to observers. His father did the same. 
But a challenge appears unlikely to succeed. 
Firstly, it seems to centre on the unprecedented decision by the Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin to extend voting nationwide by two hours. Some Bolsonaro fans are pointing out that Zanin was once Lula's lawyer and alleging bias. 
But both teams had requested an extension to voting times - Lula's had argued that voters in São Paulo and Bahia could not get to the polling stations because of a lack of buses, while Bolsonaro's campaign cited heavy rain in some areas in the south of the country and in São Paulo as their reason. 
Both knew every vote would count and did not want their side to miss out. 
The president of the Supreme Electoral Court Kássio Nunes Marques – appointed by Jair Bolsonaro – confirmed Lula's victory and said that the voter extension did not change the outcome of the race. 
The sheer gap between the two candidates' tallies - 4.4 million votes - makes the result more difficult to challenge. 
Image source, Reuters Image caption, 
Lula is making history as the first Brazilian to be elected four times 
The result came as a surprise after Flávio Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October with 47% of votes ahead of Lula's 45%. 
But Lula's camp gained momentum ahead of election day, focusing on boosting voter turnout after 33 million people did not vote in round one. 
Sunday saw the largest drop in abstention between the two rounds of a presidential election since 1989. 
Bolsonaro had been poised to give a victory speech and said the result should be annulled, calling it "inexplicable". 
As his disconsolate supporters left the house in Brasília where their candidate had been watching the result, Lula took to the streets in São Paulo to celebrate. 
"This, my fourth term, will be the best of any president in the history of this country," the former metal worker told supporters. "It will be the one in which I listen most to the Brazilian people." 
After pulling off this victory, Lula faces big hurdles: a divided country, an opponent that won't recognise the result, and a hostile Congress packed full of Bolsonaro allies. 
Markets reacted negatively to the unexpected outcome. The Sao Paolo stock exchange opened 15% down, sparking a brief suspension before recovering slightly. Interest rate futures rose as investors scrutinised Lula's fiscal plans. 
- 
Lula wins in Brazil but faces hostile Congress and divided country 
- Published 21 hours ago 
- 
How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp chat helped turn Brazil election around 
- Published 9 hours ago 
- 
Who is Lula? From ex-worker and prisoner to Brazil's president again 
- Published 13 hours ago 
Reacting to the result, US President Donald Trump suggested the election had been stolen. 
"I didn't take sides, but it looked like another rigged election," he told reporters on Monday, without providing evidence or more details. "It looked very bad to me." 
Other world leaders from across the political spectrum have congratulated Lula. Mexico's left-wing President Claudia Sheinbaum said in a post on X: "The people of Brazil won." 
Peru's right-wing President Keiko Fujimori praised Brazil's "democratic day". Similar messages were shared by the presidents of Chile and Ecuador. 
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney noted that their two countries had already "flourished under our partnership". 
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said "democracy and multilateralism" had won. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez - also a left-wing leader - called it a "great victory". 
French President Emmanuel Macron said the two nations should work "in service of a more just world". 
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa called Lula's victory one for the "global south and progressive forces throughout the world". 
Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, 
Flávio Bolsonaro has refused to accept the result, calling for it to be annulled 
In a video posted on Instagram later on Monday, Flávio Bolsonaro said police had told him to hand over his passports and had been banned from leaving the country. 
Trump has previously shown support for Bolsonaro's father Jair, who is currently serving a 27-year prison sentence after being convicted of a coup attempt after losing the 2022 elections to Lula. Flávio Bolsonaro met Trump at the White House earlier this year to bid for his support. 
Lula, who turns 81 on Tuesday, has already been president for three non-consecutive terms, serving two terms between January 2003 to December 2010, and again from January 2023. 
His win makes him the first in Brazilian history to secure a fourth term, which will last until 2030. 
But this has been a bitterly fought campaign and the new term - set to start on 5 January - comes amid significant constraints at home and abroad, including animosity from the US president. 
Referring to what Trump has called the "Donroe Doctrine" - which seeks to establish US dominance in the Western Hemisphere - Lula used his victory speech to insist that Brazil "will not accept being anyone's backyard". 
Lula has also bucked a wider trend in Latin America, where voters in countries such as Argentina, Chile and Colombia have put right-wing candidates and parties in power.

articles.title: Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic risk' to humankind ahead of blockbuster share listing
articles.summary: The company will be the first true artificial intelligence company to go public as tech firms continue to invest heavily in AI.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images By Rachel Clun ,  Business reporter ,  Liv McMahon ,  Technology reporter   and   Kali Hays ,  Technology reporter 
- Published 26 October 2026 
Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US. 
The firm's valuation is expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which was the biggest-ever listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion in the summer. 
Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be released, their price range, or a date for the listing. 
The Claude chatbot developer reported $16.3bn (£12.2bn) of revenue in the first half of the year, with losses of more than $80.7bn. 
Anthropic, which said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology. 
In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity. 
It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy". 
Anthropic was founded five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five others, and announced its intention to go public in June. 
Its main rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans. 
Those announcements were followed by a wave of cyber-security and other technological breaches involving their AI agents - bots designed to operate somewhat autonomously. 
Current and former staff of both companies also warned AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools. 
As Anthropic revealed its stock debut plans on Monday, the owners of the rights to Elvis Presley's music sued the AI firm accusing it of using hundreds of the rock-and-roll star's songs to train its chatbot Claude. 
- 
Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know 
- Published 5 hours ago 
'Bold but sane' 
In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers. 
Anthropic detailed losses in its financial filings that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance". 
"In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said. 
Its success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, Anthropic said, adding, "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business". 
Across about 90 pages detailing possible risk factors, Anthropic set out the potential threats to its ability to safely and competitively develop AI. 
Anthropic warned it relies on a cluster of cloud computing providers, Taiwanese chipmakers already facing huge demand and data centres concentrated in the US. 
It also warned of "regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models" - citing concerns over AI being used by children or individuals at risk of suicide - and uncertainty about where and how it might be held liable for actions taken by its systems. 
However, Anthropic also used the filing to laud the potential benefits of the tech itself, envisioning it unlocking "millions of virtual agents with the ability to revolutionise every area of human endeavour" across a range of fields. 
"We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," the firm said. 
Anthropic said AI would also "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine", potentially finding cures to diseases including cancer and Alzheimer's. 
The firm added it could also establish "sustained acceleration in economic growth" by boosting productivity. 
'Significant milestone' 
Matt Orton, chief market strategist at investment management firm Raymond James Investment, said investors expected to see rapid growth as well as rapid financial losses in Anthropic's finances, so Monday's filing would not come as a surprise. 
"Getting the details from this filing, I think will help provide the market with more visibility, because we need to know where its revenue growth is coming from," he told the BBC. 
Peter Andersen, founder of Andersen Capital Management, told Reuters that Anthropic's plans to list was "a significant milestone in the development of artificial intelligence". 
He added that the outcome of its stock market debut would be "fairly indicative of the sentiment" among investors to continue ploughing cash into AI development.

articles.title: Who is Lula? From ex-worker and prisoner to Brazil's president again
articles.summary: The firebrand left-winger, who has at times been at odds with Trump, has won his fourth term as Brazil's president.
articles.full_text:
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Even for a veteran politician like Lula, uniting a divided nation will be a challenge By Paulin Kola 
- Published 26 October 2026 
On the face of it, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has done the impossible one more time - within three weeks he overturned defeat in first-round voting to gain re-election as Brazil's president. 
It was no mean achievement for a man who before his first successful run at the post in 2002 had tried three times unsuccessfully. 
When he became president in 2003, he came to office as the first leftist leader of Brazil in nearly half a century. 
Now aged 80 and with plenty of experience at governing as large a democracy as Brazil, he has bucked the trend of electoral victory for right-wing leaders in Latin America whose policies mirror that of US President Donald Trump. 
Figure caption, 
Who is Lula and what are his policies? 
Lula's first presidential victory in 2002 marked the end of an unprecedented journey from poverty. 
The son of a poor, illiterate peasant family, Lula worked as a peanut seller and shoe-shine boy as a child, only learning to read when he was 10 years old. 
He went on to train as a metalworker and found work in an industrial city near São Paulo, where he lost the little finger of his left hand in an accident in the 1960s. 
Lula was not initially interested in politics, but threw himself into trade union activism. 
Elected leader of the 100,000-strong Metalworkers' Union in 1975, he transformed trade union activism in Brazil by turning what had mostly been government-friendly organisations into a powerful independent movement. 
In 1980, Lula brought together a combination of trade unionists, intellectuals, Trotskyites and Church activists to found the Workers' Party (PT), the first major socialist party in the country's history. 
The PT went on to gradually replace its revolutionary commitment to changing the power structure in Brazil with a more pragmatic, social democratic platform. 
Lula came to power promising major reforms to the country's political and economic system. 
He vowed to eradicate hunger and create a self-confident, caring, outward-looking nation. 
Image source, Wojtek Laski/Getty Images Image caption, 
In this picture Lula is seen meeting fellow Polish trade unionist - and subsequently president - Lech Walesa in Rome, Italy, in 1981 
In his time in office, Lula pumped billions of dollars into social programmes and can reasonably claim to have helped reverse Brazil's historic inequalities. 
By increasing the minimum wage well above the rate of inflation and broadening state help to the most impoverished with a family grant programme, the Bolsa Familia, he helped some 44 million people and cemented his support among the poor. 
However, many commentators argue that the programme failed to address the structural problems that underpin poverty, such as a lack of education. 
He left office eight years later, after serving two terms as president, enjoying exceptionally high popularity ratings for a retiring Latin American leader - 83% - having raised Brazil's profile on the international scene and presided over the longest period of economic growth in three decades. 
Unable to run for a third term, Lula left the presidency and, shortly afterwards, was diagnosed with throat cancer. He even shaved his trademark beard during treatment. Doctors declared him cured of the disease in 2012. 
- 
Lula wins fourth term in dramatic Brazil election comeback 
- Published 4 hours ago 
- 
Lula faces hostile congress and divided country after Brazil election win 
- Published 21 hours ago 
Why was Lula previously jailed? 
Under his chosen successor, progress stalled. The economic boom also gave way to recession, and the country's political scene was rocked by a huge investigation into top-level corruption, known as Operation Car Wash. 
Lula was among those to get caught up in the scandal. In July 2017, he was convicted of corruption and sentenced to more than nine years in prison for accepting a beachside flat as a bribe from engineering firm OAS - a sentence increased on appeal to 12 years. 
Lula was also jailed for 12 years and 11 months for corruption and money laundering for receiving bribes from two construction and engineering firms by way of funding improvements in a country house he and his family used. 
He has always maintained his innocence, insisting accusations against him were politically motivated. 
In 2019, he was released after having served just over 18 months, after a Supreme Court ruling that the incarceration had been illegal, having come before all appeals had been exhausted. 
Those convictions were annulled in 2021, leaving Lula free to run for a third term in 2022, beating right-winger Jair Bolsonaro. 
When he re-entered office in 2023, he vowed it would be his last term, and yet his party endorsed him as their candidate again this year, even though he will turn 81 on Tuesday. 
Even backers of the PT will acknowledge that he achieved more in his first two terms - from January 2003 to December 2010 - than in his most recent four years in office. 
And while his supporters described him ahead of the 2022 election as the "saviour of the Amazon", praising his commitment to protecting the rainforest, some environmentalists have been critical of some of his recent actions. 
His support for exploratory oil drilling in offshore waters near the mouth of the Amazon in particular has drawn criticism. 
Lula insists that he remains committed to eventually phasing out fossil fuels and argues that oil revenues are key to financing Brazil's transition to clean energy. 
His government has also pointed to the reduction in deforestation in the Amazon - satellite data suggests the area deforested in the first half of 2026 was reduced to its lowest in the past decade - as proof that its policies were working. 
What is Lula's relationship with Trump? 
Lula's third term coincided with the return to office of Trump. 
The two men represent different ends of the political spectrum and have found it impossible not to voice their differences in public. 
The Brazilian leader told the BBC in September 2025 that he had no relationship with Trump . 
Even though the US has a trade surplus with Brazil, Donald Trump imposed 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods in July that year, citing the trial on coup charges of Brazil's right-wing former president Jair Bolsonaro as a trigger. Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year jail sentence and it was his son, Flávio, who Lula beat in Sunday's election run-off. 
Lula accused Trump of foreign interference and said "he's not emperor of the world". But their relationship improved after a White House in May this year, after which the two leaders exchanged public compliments - Trump called Lula "dynamic", while the Brazilian president said he left the meeting "very satisfied". 
In July of this year, the US imposed 25% tariffs on most goods , external from Brazil. 
The two governments still disagree on key issues such as crime, and Lula acknowledged they are especially far apart on trade. 
Referring to what Trump has dubbed the "Donroe doctrine" - his administration's national security strategy which asserts that US dominance in the Western hemisphere should not be interfered with - Lula has insisted that "Brazil does not fit into anyone's backyard". 
Image source, Getty Images Image caption, 
Trump and Lula had warm words when they met in Washington earlier this year 
Is Lula close to China and Russia? 
Lula has criticised the fact that five countries - the permanent members of the UN Security Council - have the power to veto decisions and argued that this tilted the balance in favour of those who won World War Two, excluding nations representing billions of people like Brazil, Germany, India, and Japan, as well as African countries. 
Brazil is an active member of the Brics - a grouping that unites Brazil with Russia, India, China and South Africa. 
Lula defends his continued alliances with Russia and China and sees the Brics as an emerging counterweight to the West. 
He has defended his choice to continue to purchase Russian oil while Russia wages war in Ukraine.

‘Zero-energy companionship’: bizarre hobby takes seed among China’s stressed young adults
Faced with a stagnant jobs market, many are spurning children or pets in favour of ‘raising bricks’ 
Young adults in China looking for a cheaper, low-maintenance alternative to having children or pets have found an answer: raising bricks. 
Bricks may not be as cuddly as cats or as life-affirming as human offspring, but they also cost next to nothing. “No cats, no dating, I started raising a brick,” wrote one brick parent on social media. 
Raising “brick babies” is easier than caring for house plants, involving spraying them with water a few times a day then waiting for moss spores already present in the atmosphere to attach themselves and grow. One Chinese media article described the bricks as being “practically immortal”. “If you forget to water them, the moss goes dormant. If you remember to water them again, the greenery returns.” 
A hashtag related to the trend has attracted more than 5m views on the Chinese social media platform Weibo. 
View image in fullscreen 
Social media users document their brick’s changes over a year, with hashtags including #healing and #stress relief. Photograph: @South/xiaohongshu.com 
Chinese commentators have linked the trend to young people looking for low-effort routes to finding meaning in life. One brick “parent” told Chinese media the hobby created “a sense of accomplishment no less than completing a long-term project”. 
One user on Xiaohongshu, an Instagram-like platform, also known as Rednote, posted a picture of their rusty-coloured brick, saying “no output required, no KPIs to hit, no need to beg it to bloom [and] no comparing its growth with others”. 
Another user wrote: “My friends asked if I’d lost my mind. I said no, I’m just starting to raise a brick. 
“A brick gives me a sense of certainty that feels way more grounded than a lot of relationships. Psychologists call this ‘zero-energy emotional companionship.’ It fulfils your need for company without demanding any obligation to give love in return.” 
Young people in China are increasingly shunning the traditional expectations of society, such as having children and working long hours in strenuous jobs, assuming they can find one in the first place. Nearly one in five 16- to 24-year-olds, excluding students, are unemployed , according to official statistics. Some estimates put the unemployment rate much higher. 
China’s birthrate is in decline and fell to a record low last year. Faced with a sluggish job market after years of intensely competitive studying, many young people are choosing to shun the rat race and opt instead for “ lying flat ” – pursuing a low-effort, low-stress lifestyle; one well-suited to raising bricks. 
The trend has become so popular that Chinese media have started to warn about the health risks. 
Cultivating moss could lead to the spread of mould, with some “brick parents” reportedly complaining of itchy eyes and runny noses. Xuedong Li, a retired professor of moss from Beijing’s Capital Normal University, urged people to keep their bricks in an enclosed environment. “It is best to wear disposable gloves and a mask during handling to reduce spore inhalation and skin contact,” Li told Chinese media.
